articles.headline: OFAC Issues International Criminal Court Designation and General Licenses, Removes Burma-Related Designation
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a new designation related to the International Criminal Court (ICC) on October 9, 2026. This action was accompanied by the issuance of new General Licenses to guide permissible activities.
In a separate but concurrent action, OFAC also announced the removal of a Burma-related designation. This indicates a targeted adjustment to the sanctions program concerning Myanmar.
Additionally, OFAC published a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics on the same date, addressing a separate enforcement matter.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a new Russia-related General License on October 9, 2026. This license outlines specific transactions or activities that are permitted under the existing Russia sanctions program.

General Licenses are frequently used by OFAC to clarify the scope of sanctions and to authorize certain humanitarian, administrative, or other specific types of transactions that would otherwise be prohibited.
This issuance follows a period of ongoing adjustments to the Russia sanctions regime, reflecting the dynamic nature of U.S. foreign policy responses.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-Related Designations, Issues General Licenses for Iran and Amends Russia-Related License
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 8, 2026, intensifying economic pressure on Tehran.
These designations were accompanied by the issuance of a new Iran-related General License, which typically outlines permissible transactions or activities under the updated sanctions program.
In a related action, OFAC also issued an amended Russia-related General License, indicating ongoing adjustments and clarifications to the sanctions targeting Russia.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Designations Removals and Updates, Publishes Iran-Related Alert and Amended FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced several designations removals and updates on October 5, 2026, indicating a recalibration of its sanctions lists.

In conjunction with these changes, OFAC published an Iran-related Alert, likely providing guidance or warnings regarding specific activities or entities. An amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) was also released, offering further clarification on existing sanctions policy.
These actions reflect OFAC's continuous effort to maintain and refine its sanctions programs, ensuring they remain effective and transparent.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Counter Terrorism Designations on October 2, 2026. These designations target individuals and entities involved in terrorist activities, aiming to disrupt their financial networks.
Such actions are a critical component of the U.S. government's broader strategy to combat global terrorism by cutting off access to financial resources.
The specific individuals and entities designated were added to OFAC's Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons (SDN) List, imposing comprehensive prohibitions on transactions with them.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Iran-Related Designations and Updates, Transnational Criminal Organizations Designation, and Iran-Related Guidance
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) implemented new Iran-related designations and designations updates on October 1, 2026, as part of its ongoing efforts to counter Iranian illicit activities.

Concurrently, OFAC announced a Transnational Criminal Organizations Designation, targeting entities involved in international criminal enterprises. This highlights the intersection of sanctions policy with broader law enforcement objectives.
The agency also published an Iran-related Determination and an Amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question, providing further clarity and legal basis for the new measures and existing policies.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Terrorism and Transnational Criminal Organizations Designations, Removes Belarus, Counter Narcotics, and Libya Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Counter Terrorism and Transnational Criminal Organizations Designations on September 30, 2026, targeting individuals and entities involved in illicit global activities.

In a separate set of actions, OFAC also announced the removal of several designations related to Belarus, Counter Narcotics programs, and Libya. These removals indicate a reassessment of specific sanctions targets within these programs.

These simultaneous actions demonstrate OFAC's dynamic approach to sanctions, involving both the imposition of new restrictions and the removal of existing ones based on evolving circumstances and policy objectives.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Counter Narcotics, Counter Terrorism, Iran-Related, and Non-Proliferation Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a broad range of new designations on September 29, 2026, targeting illicit activities across multiple sanctions programs. These include designations under Counter Narcotics, Counter Terrorism, Iran-related, and Non-Proliferation authorities.
The Iran-related designations are part of the ongoing 'Operation Economic Outcast' which aims to disrupt Iran's oil trade and sanctions-evasion networks.
This comprehensive action underscores the U.S. government's commitment to combating various threats to national security and foreign policy interests through economic sanctions.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / The National Law Review

articles.headline: OFAC Publishes Regulatory Amendments and New Cuba Sanctions Regulations, Issues New and Amended FAQs and Alert
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) published significant regulatory amendments and new Cuba Sanctions Regulations on September 29, 2026. These new regulations implement Executive Order 14404 of May 1, 2026, which imposes sanctions on those responsible for repression in Cuba and threats to U.S. national security and foreign policy.

In conjunction with these regulatory changes, OFAC issued new and amended Cuba-related Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) to provide guidance on the updated policies. A Cuba-related OFAC Alert was also published, likely highlighting specific risks or compliance considerations.
These actions signify a tightening of U.S. sanctions policy towards Cuba, reflecting ongoing concerns regarding human rights and national security.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / The National Law Review

Companies operating under Venezuela authorizations should carefully review the revised terms to ensure ongoing compliance.

articles.headline: Federal Reserve Signals Further Rate Hikes as Inflation Persists
body: The U.S. Federal Reserve's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) raised the policy rate by 0.25 percentage point at its September meeting, with additional hikes likely in the coming months to cool the economy and maintain inflation-fighting credibility.

Inflation expectations have remained broadly stable this year, though still above pre-COVID-19 norms. Core Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price inflation, excluding energy and food, was estimated at 3.4 percent in August, higher than a year earlier.

The Fed is closely monitoring the effects of the energy price shock on inflation, with projections indicating total inflation to be 3.6 percent in August and core inflation at 3.2 percent under a new methodology.

articles.headline: OCC Assesses $350 Million Penalty Against American Express National Bank for BSA/AML Failures
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced a cease-and-desist order and a $350 million civil money penalty against American Express National Bank for significant deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and anti-money laundering (AML) compliance program.

The OCC identified inadequate resources, insufficient staff expertise, systemic internal control gaps, weak independent testing, and a failure to tailor its BSA/AML risk assessment to its business activities, particularly its dominant credit and charge card products.

These compliance breakdowns led to a failure to timely identify, evaluate, and report approximately $13 billion of suspected trade-based money laundering activity over the past decade. The OCC's action is coordinated with a concurrent cease-and-desist order by the Federal Reserve System.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency / Banking Dive

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
